column2: Finding people who are missing or trapped after a disaster and bringing them to safety.
A sudden shaking of the ground caused by movement along a fault in the Earth's crust.
Planning and coordinating the work before, during and after a disaster: preparedness, response and recovery.
A smaller earthquake that follows the main shock in the same area, sometimes for weeks.
Broken concrete, masonry and other remains of a collapsed or damaged building.
A sudden, dangerous situation that needs immediate action.
A safe place that protects people from weather and danger after they lose their homes.
The area affected by an earthquake.
Housing such as containers or prefabricated units where survivors live until permanent homes are ready.
A machine that lifts and moves heavy loads such as concrete slabs.
Water covering land that is normally dry.
Unable to get out, for example under rubble or in a closed space.
Ready-to-eat food packed for one person for a set period.
A thin reflective foil blanket that keeps body heat in; also called a space blanket.
A trained group that searches for and frees trapped people.
A camera that shows heat, used to find people in the dark, in smoke or under rubble.
A hard hat that protects the head from falling objects.
A set of straps worn around the waist and legs to attach a person to a rope.
To move everyone out of a dangerous area.
The place where an accident or disaster happened and where responders work.
The planned way people follow to leave a dangerous area.
A marked exit used to leave a building quickly in danger.
A building, or part of one, that has fallen down.
Clearing the rubble of collapsed buildings from a site.
To find the exact place where a person or thing is.
A plan for restoring services, housing and normal life after a disaster.
The sudden failure of a building's structure, so that it falls.
A horizontal structural member that carries the load of a floor or roof to the columns.
A vertical structural member that carries the building's weight down to the foundation.
Concrete strengthened with steel bars; the most common structural material of modern buildings.
A temporary element that holds up a damaged structure so that it does not move or fall.
To place supports under or against an unstable structure.
A tapered block, usually of wood, driven into a gap to hold or lift a load.
A strong synthetic (nylon) rope material used in climbing and rescue.
A tool for lifting heavy loads a short distance.
A metal loop with a spring gate, used to connect ropes and harnesses quickly.
A D-shaped metal ring on a harness or strap to which ropes and carabiners are attached.
A lanyard with a built-in element that stretches to reduce the force of a fall.
A device that locks on a rope or rail and stops a person who falls.
A metal device shaped like the number 8, used to control a rope when lowering or abseiling.
A bolt with a ring at one end, used as an anchor point for ropes or lifting.
A rope clamp that slides up a rope but locks when pulled down, used for climbing a rope.
A device with sensors that detects sounds and vibrations made by people trapped under rubble.
A powerful drill that hammers while it turns, used to drill into concrete.
Removing water from a flooded place.
The parts of a building (columns, beams, walls, foundation) that carry its weight.
A quick survey of what affected people need, such as water, food, shelter and medical care.
Information that gives the location of a person, vehicle or site, for example GPS coordinates.
An abnormal rise of the sea along the coast, for example a storm surge or tsunami.
The point on the Earth's surface directly above the place where an earthquake starts.
Many small earthquakes in the same area over a short time, without one clear main shock.
A fracture in the Earth's crust along which the rock on either side moves.
A long-handled cutter for steel bars, bolts and chains.
A lamp worn on the head or helmet, leaving both hands free.
A portable motor saw with a toothed chain, used to cut wood.
Basic, immediate shelter given to people right after a disaster.
The protective action during an earthquake: get down, take cover under sturdy furniture and hold on to it.
A hand-held power tool with a fast-turning disc, used to cut or grind metal and concrete.
A layer of ice forming on a surface such as a road.
A crack in a wall, column or other building element.
A temporary support built by stacking timber blocks in crossed layers under a load.
An inflatable cushion placed under a heavy load and filled with air to lift it.
A device that detects signs of life, such as breathing or movement, under rubble.
A construction machine with a bucket on an arm, used to dig and to remove rubble.
A tool driven by compressed air that breaks concrete and rock.
A metal bottle that holds gas under pressure.
The immediate actions taken to save lives and protect people after an incident.
A computer system that collects and shares information for managing disasters.
The officer in charge of operations in a disaster area.
A tent used to house people who lost their homes in a disaster.
The repeating phases of disaster management: mitigation, preparedness, response and recovery.
A person who helps in disaster work without being paid, usually after training.
An office that coordinates communication between the organisations working in a disaster.
Moving and storing the people, equipment and supplies needed in a disaster.
A bag packed in advance with what a person needs for the first 72 hours of an emergency.
A written plan that says who does what when a disaster or emergency happens.
Türkiye's national agency for disaster and emergency management (AFAD).
Damage so serious that a building is unsafe and cannot be used.
A package of food meant to feed one family for a set time.
A fault that has moved in recent geological time and can cause earthquakes.
A large, heavy hammer swung with both hands to break concrete or masonry.
The ground area that a building covers.
Neighbouring buildings hitting each other during an earthquake because the gap between them is too small.
Food that keeps without refrigeration, such as rice, pasta, flour and pulses.
A simple stove that burns compressed sawdust.
A wood-burning stove that is also used for cooking.
A stove that burns small compressed wood pellets.
A portable heater that burns kerosene (paraffin).
A fuel gas (propane and butane) stored as a liquid under pressure; used for cooking and heating.
Natural gas stored at high pressure, used as a fuel.
A metal container holding burning coal or wood, used outdoors for warmth.
A device, such as ground-penetrating radar, that shows what lies under the ground or rubble.
A power saw with a diamond blade or chain for cutting concrete.
A zone of the Earth where earthquakes happen often.
How long the ground shakes during an earthquake.
The strength of the shaking at a particular place, judged by its effects on people and buildings.
A building technique that separates a structure from ground shaking, usually with flexible bearings.
Stocks of food and other basic goods.
Health care brought to people by vehicles or teams that travel, instead of a fixed clinic.
An area declared safe from danger, where people can gather.
A line of people or barriers that keeps the public out of a dangerous area.
Damage that does not affect the safety of a building; it can still be used.
To tell the authorities officially that something has happened.
Heavy machines used in building work, such as excavators, loaders and cranes.
A smaller earthquake that comes before a larger one in the same place.
An instrument that records the shaking of the ground.
Moving people out of a dangerous place to a safe one.
Türkiye's Ministry of Health teams of medical staff trained for rescue in disasters (UMKE).
A cloth in which a dead body is wrapped for burial.
The prayer or religious ceremony held for a person who has died, before burial.
The official who governs a district (ilçe) in Türkiye, appointed by the state.
A grave in which many bodies are buried together.
The elected head of a village or neighbourhood in Türkiye.
The area that a disaster has affected.
A wall that holds back soil on a slope.
A dog trained to find people who are missing or trapped.
To stay in a place that gives protection.
A material burned to produce heat or power, such as petrol, diesel, gas, coal or wood.
Broken pieces of building material.
The remains of buildings that have collapsed.
Ground made by filling a site with soil or waste; it shakes more strongly in an earthquake than natural ground.
An electric tool that breaks concrete with repeated blows.
A device that mixes gas (acetylene, natural gas or propane) with air or oxygen to make a flame.
A building that shares side walls with the buildings next to it.
A building that stands alone, not touching others.
A building joined to one other building on one side.
A lane that drivers keep clear so that emergency vehicles can pass.
A shaking of the ground; a short earthquake.
A building where goods and supplies are stored.
A temporary hospital set up in tents or containers near a disaster or conflict.
A movable toilet cabin that needs no sewer connection.
A steel bar with a flattened, curved end, used to lever objects apart.
A hydraulic prop that holds up or stabilises a load.
A torch that cuts metal with a very hot flame.
A hydraulic cylinder that pushes with great force, used to move or hold apart heavy parts.
A hydraulic tool with strong blades that cuts metal.
A hydraulic tool whose arms open with great force to separate or lift parts.
Tools driven by an electric motor, such as drills and saws.
A United Nations network that sets the standards for international urban search and rescue teams (INSARAG).
